strengths: The main case for weak acceptance is the task-and-dataset contribution. AVIS combines sound-conditioned segmentation with persistent instance identities, addressing a meaningful limitation of semantic audio-visual segmentation. AVISeg provides 94,074 masks across 926 videos averaging 61.4 seconds, covering 26 categories; 59.16% of annotated frames contain multiple sound sources.

The baseline has supported empirical value. Under the stated common ResNet-50 backbone and training budget, AVISM improves over COMBO from 57.39 to 61.73 HOTA and from 37.84 to 40.57 mAP (Table 2). These established metrics support the contribution independently of concerns about the proposed FSLA metric.

The ablations demonstrate useful incremental effects of audio fusion. Adding frame-level fusion raises HOTA from 57.48 to 59.59, and subsequently adding video-level fusion reaches 61.73 (Table 4). Window-size, backbone, pretraining, and similarity-loss experiments provide additional technical support.

The architecture is understandable and appropriately acknowledges its Mask2Former/VITA foundations. The supplementary material provides useful training settings, baseline prompts, qualitative comparisons, and explicit failure cases involving multiple same-category sources. Although algorithmic originality is modest, the resulting baseline is useful for establishing this benchmark.
weaknesses: FSLA is not specified reproducibly. Supplementary Algorithm 1 counts silent frames as correct without checking predictions, initializes success counters outside the IoU-threshold loop, and does not explicitly enforce the required equality of object counts. Its aggregation also omits the class averaging described in Section 3.2. These may be pseudocode errors, but the supplied algorithm cannot explain the reported scores. This materially weakens the metric contribution without establishing that HOTA or mAP results are incorrect.

The evidence for annotation reliability is incomplete for the task's distinctive supervision. Section 4 reports SAM-assisted annotation and repeated manual review, but provides no quantitative agreement audit or explicit procedure for adjudicating ambiguous sound attribution among similar instances. Accurate mask boundaries alone do not establish accurate sound-to-instance labels. The random video split also lacks documentation of source-level duplicate controls; this leaves independence insufficiently documented, rather than demonstrating leakage.

The broad conclusions about multimodal large models exceed what their adaptations establish. Supplementary Sections E.1–E.2 merge same-category masks across a video into one object, and E.4 treats each category as one instance. Sam4AVS additionally selects only the top audio category per segment. These choices structurally restrict performance on multiple-instance scenes, so the results characterize these particular pipelines and do not isolate the underlying models' instance or temporal reasoning capabilities.

Evidence for the emphasized same-category and long-range capabilities remains limited. Figure 10 documents failures with similar sounding instances, but aggregate results do not quantify performance specifically on that subset. Table 5 demonstrates frame capacity, not tracking accuracy at those maximum lengths, and provides no comparative runtime or memory measurements. Evaluation at 1 FPS also limits conclusions about rapid sound transitions. These reservations constrain the claims, while the dataset and improvements on established metrics still provide a stronger case for acceptance.
